text: You have seen a cactus many times, but have you ever seen its leaves? Miss this, and you lose easy exam marks. So where are they?

Hi there, and welcome to The One App, Explained! I'm so happy you're here. Today, you will learn three big ideas. First, different kinds of stems. Second, plants with amazing superpowers. And third, different kinds of roots. Let's get started!

Last time, we learnt that leaves make food, the stem holds the plant up and carries things, and roots anchor and absorb. But plants live in very different places. So their parts can look very different, even when they do similar jobs. Let's meet some plants with superpowers.
First, stems. Some stems are hard and woody. Trees have thick woody stems, and shrubs have thinner woody stems. People even use woody stems as firewood, and to build log cabins.

Other stems are soft. These are non-woody stems, like the herbs mint and parsley. And some stems do extra work. The baobab tree grows in very dry places. It stores water in its huge stem, so it can survive the long dry season.
Now, the cactus. Those sharp spines? They are its leaves! Spines help the cactus lose less water, and they protect it from hungry animals.
But if the leaves are spines, what makes the food? The green stem does! In a cactus, the stem makes food for the plant.

Some plants have weak, soft stems that cannot hold them up. So they use a superpower. Climbers coil around poles, fences or other plants, and climb up towards the light. Creepers spread out along the ground, and fan out their leaves to catch as much light as they can.
Roots can be different too. Water lettuce floats on ponds, with hairy-looking roots hanging down in the water. A giant rain tree has strong, sturdy roots that grip the soil.
And some roots store food. Carrots, turnips and sweet potatoes are storage roots. They keep the food that the leaves made, so the plant can use it later.

Sweet potato is a superstar. It is easy to grow, it keeps longer than leafy vegetables, and it can even replace rice when food is short. That is why community gardens in Singapore grow food like this, to help the country grow more of its own food.

Here is a plant magic trick. Ask an adult to help you cut a piece of stem, called a stem cutting, and stand it in a glass of water. After a few days, new roots start to grow. Plant it in soil, and it becomes a whole new plant.

One scientist who loved plants was Henry Ridley, the first director of the Singapore Botanic Gardens. He kept on trying, until he found a way to collect latex from rubber trees without harming them. His idea helped to build the rubber industry across the region. That is perseverance.
Pause and predict! This plant is wrapped around a pole. What does that tell you about its stem?
Its stem is weak and non-woody. It climbs the pole to reach more light, so its leaves can make more food.

In your exam, say it like this. In a cactus, the spines are leaves, and they reduce water loss. The green stem makes food. A climbing plant has a weak stem, and it climbs to get more light to make food. Storage roots, like carrots, store food.
Here is a habit to try. Make it satisfying. Every time you learn a new plant fact, give yourself a tick on a habit tracker. Watching your ticks grow feels great, so you will want to keep going.

Then grow your mind map. Plant parts in the middle. Leaves, including spines. Stems, woody, non-woody and climbing. Roots, for storage and for water. Then save it in TheOneApp, the ultimate science app.
So, where are the cactus leaves? They are the spines! Your turn. Look around your home or school. Can you spot a climber, a creeper or a storage root? Tell me in the comments.
Thanks for watching! See you next time. Bye!
